fatal_errors: The hypothesis assumes without evidence that increasing constituent count increases short-range order and makes the quinary alloy stronger than every quaternary and ternary subset.

The predicted universal superiority of the quinary alloy conflicts with the target composition dependence, in which strength tracks local lattice distortion/MSAD and a Cr-containing quaternary has the highest extrapolated 0 K CRSS.
Ambient-temperature testing alone cannot explain the principal cryogenic inertial dulling and high-temperature Portevin-Le Chatelier behavior that distinguish deformation across the studied alloys.

The proposed evidence does not establish enhanced SRO in this specific Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni compositional series; E1 concerns Pd substitution and explicitly notes an alternative misfit-volume explanation, while E2 provides no comparative SRO evidence.
explanation: This is a testable alternative centered on local chemical order rather than constituent count, and its controlled processing, microscopy, mechanical measurements, and explicit falsification rule give it some scientific value. However, it reconstructs neither the single-crystal [1̄23] compression program nor the temperature-, rate-, and composition-dependent measurements in the target. The target attributes low-temperature strength primarily to MSAD-controlled solid-solution resistance with phonon-drag-related inertial dulling, and high-temperature strengthening to Mn/Fe-dependent dynamic solute pinning. The generated hypothesis instead predicts an unsupported monotonic constituent-count hierarchy and focuses only on room-temperature yield and work hardening. Its experiment could detect correlations, but it does not cleanly distinguish SRO from ordinary size/misfit-driven lattice distortion unless SRO is independently manipulated at fixed composition and initial defect structure.
